issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may not set aside concurrent factual findings merely because it prefers a different view of the evidence; reappraisal is limited to determining whether the fact-finding court’s conclusion is wholly unreasonable.
material_facts: The rent-control court rejected the landlords’ grounds of rent default, nuisance, and damage, and the appellate authority affirmed those findings.
The lower courts considered evidence bearing on the alleged rent increase, including the landlords’ reply notice, tax and income records, and rent receipts they found unconvincing.

The lower courts found that the machinery had been used in the building for many years, that the alleged noise and damage did not establish the eviction grounds, and that the observed physical defects were trivial.
The High Court reversed the concurrent findings and granted eviction, stating generally that the lower courts had ignored evidence, without adequately addressing their reasoning or the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction by reversing the concurrent findings in this manner. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court’s judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 22 of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 confers supervisory revisional jurisdiction to examine the legality, regularity, or propriety of an order; it does not equate revision with an appeal. Under Sarla Ahuja v. United India Insurance Company Limited, reappraisal of evidence in revision is permissible only to determine whether the fact-finding court’s conclusion is wholly unreasonable. Sri Raj Lakshmi Dyeing Works v. Rangaswamy likewise establishes that a revisional court should not interfere with factual findings merely because it disagrees with them.

rule.if: appeal_from_rent_eviction_revision and concurrent_factual_findings and findings_supported_by_evidence and revisional_reversal_without_adequate_reasoning

predicates.appeal_from_rent_eviction_revision: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a revisional court’s decision in a rent-based eviction case.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The initial fact-finding court and the appellate authority reached the same factual conclusions.
predicates.findings_supported_by_evidence: The concurrent conclusions were based on evidence considered by the lower courts.
predicates.revisional_reversal_without_adequate_rea: The revisional court reversed the concurrent conclusions without adequately addressing the lower courts’ reasoning and the evidence they considered.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an eviction revision, the lower courts reached concurrent evidence-based findings, and the revisional court reversed them without adequate reasoning, the reversal is unjustified.

issues.legal_issue: The nuisance ground for eviction requires actionable private nuisance involving substantial or reasonably perceptible interference, not merely ordinary inconvenience or noise.
material_facts: The landlords alleged that the tenant quarrelled with them when they sought rent and operated machinery late at night, disturbing other occupants.
The machinery had been installed and operated in the building for many years, and the tenant had conducted the same business there during that time.
The lower courts found no evidence of a complaint about nuisance before the eviction petition and concluded that the alleged conduct did not establish nuisance.
The High Court reversed those findings without adequately considering the limits of its revisional jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not establish the nuisance ground for eviction, and the High Court could not properly displace the concurrent findings in the manner it did.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(2)(iv) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 concerns nuisance to occupants of other portions of the same building or buildings in the neighbourhood, meaning private rather than public nuisance. As described in Halsbury’s Laws of England, nuisance requires an unlawful interference with the use or enjoyment of land and actual or presumed damage; damage must be material or substantial, not trivial, fleeting, or merely sentimental. Ordinary inconvenience or noise is insufficient without reasonably perceptible interference.

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns eviction of a tenant from rented premises.
predicates.alleged_interference_is_not_substantial: The alleged conduct causes no material or reasonably perceptible interference with other occupants’ use or enjoyment of their property.
predicates.longstanding_activity_without_prior_comp: The activity had been carried on for a substantial time and no complaint about it was made before the eviction dispute arose.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding, if the alleged interference is not substantial and the longstanding activity drew no prior complaints, the nuisance ground for eviction is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s act of waste warrants eviction only when it is reasonably probable to impair the building’s value or utility to a material and substantial degree.
material_facts: An Advocate-Commissioner reported uneven concrete flooring, a hole in the floor for a pipe, nail-holes, no damage to the roof or walls, and only slight vibration at the parapet while the machinery operated.
The rent-control court and appellate authority found the observed defects trivial and concluded that they would not affect the building’s value or utility.
The High Court treated the holes and spaces between the shutter and wall as proof of qualifying damage, displacing the concurrent findings.
issues.conclusion: The observed defects did not establish acts of waste likely to materially impair the building’s value or utility, and the High Court improperly substituted its findings for those of the lower courts.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(2)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 requires acts of waste likely to impair materially the value or utility of the building. The impairment must be reasonably probable and substantial. In Om Pal v. Anand Swarup, the Court held that material impairment must substantially diminish value or utility and that the landlord bears the burden of proving it.

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns eviction of a tenant from rented premises.
predicates.alleged_building_damage_is_trivial: The observed defects to the building are minor rather than substantial.
predicates.no_reasonably_probable_material_impairme: The evidence does not show that the defects are reasonably likely to substantially reduce the building’s value or utility.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding, if the alleged building damage is trivial and is not reasonably likely to cause material impairment, the waste ground for eviction is not established.
